claims.text: The elevated-temperature stability of nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal HENA is not governed solely by configurational entropy.
Suppressing brittle intermetallic formation and maintaining a coherent solid-solution matrix are critical to HENA stability.
Prior solid-solution formation criteria specify −20 ≤ ΔH_mix ≤ 5 kJ/mol, 12 ≤ ΔS_mix ≤ 17.5 J/(K·mol), and δ ≤ 6.4%.
Exceeding δ = 6.4% or having sufficiently negative ΔH_mix favors ordering or loss of the solid solution.
Violation of the δ or ΔH_mix constraints causes rapid coarsening, brittle-phase precipitation, and structural collapse in HENA nanoparticles.
A nearly equiatomic Nb-Mo-Ta-W-X nanoparticle with X equal to Cr or Ti can be prepared initially as a single-phase solid solution below 50 nm.
Mechanical milling or sputtering can produce the specified single-phase quinary nanoparticles.
For the proposed alloys, 0.5–0.8 Tm corresponds to approximately 900–1400 °C.
Annealing the target HENA can form C14 Laves, B2, or L21 phases.
Atomic diffusion reduces coherent lattice strain and thereby mediates degradation from the initial solid solution.
Configurational entropy above 1.5R theoretically stabilizes a solid solution.
The thermodynamic driving force for phase separation can overcome sluggish diffusion in these nanoparticles.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles amplifies the driving forces for coarsening and phase separation.
C14 Laves phases are brittle and deteriorate properties by increasing the tendency to crack.
Nanoparticles with δ > 6.4% or ΔH_mix < −20 kJ/mol will show rapid grain growth, brittle precipitation, and significant losses of yield strength and ductility at elevated temperature.
Nanoparticles satisfying the solid-solution criteria will retain a single-phase structure and high strength after annealing.
Bulk refractory high-entropy alloys commonly have high thermal stability and elevated-temperature strength.
Bulk high-entropy alloys often exhibit sluggish diffusion.
Surface-energy effects become negligible when the nanoparticle size exceeds 100 nm.
Electronic effects can stabilize solid solutions at high δ values in ways not captured by the simple δ and ΔH_mix criteria.

contradictions.description: The intervention defines the annealing range as 900–1400 °C, whereas the conditions extend it to 900–1600 °C, leaving the intended upper temperature boundary inconsistent.
